analysis.one_liner: Replaces income taxes with a flat 15% tax, repeals the estate tax, and cuts federal spending.
analysis.headline: A one-sponsor bill to impose a 15% flat tax, end all taxes on investment income and inheritances, and cut federal spending by 15% died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Jesse Helms's bill would have replaced the graduated income tax with a single 15% tax on wages and business profits, with the first $20,000 for a married couple exempted. It would have stopped taxing capital gains, dividends, and interest entirely, repealed the estate tax, and cut most federal spending by 15% through 1998 — protecting only Social Security, Medicare, and veterans' programs. It also would have abolished the IRS and moved its duties to the Treasury Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy households gain the most: investment income (capital gains, dividends, interest) would go completely untaxed, the estate tax on large inheritances disappears, and the top wage rate falls from 39.6% to 15%. Businesses gain a 15% tax on active income with no separate corporate layer. Lower-wage workers would also pay little or nothing on wages below the exemption, and voluntary tips would go untaxed — but that group was not the bill's center of gravity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy households, large estates, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: A single 15% rate on wages and business profit, with no individual tax at all on capital gains, dividends, or interest — the main income sources of the wealthiest households.
Full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes on inherited wealth.
Repeal of nearly every deduction, exclusion, and credit, keeping only a transition rule for interest on mortgages taken out before enactment.

A 15% cut in discretionary spending and a cut of direct spending to 85% of its 1995 level for everything except Social Security, Medicare, and veterans' programs, with foreign aid falling to 40% of its 1995 level by 1998.
Wages up to the exemption ($20,000 joint, $10,000 single, plus $5,000 per dependent) would be tax-free, and voluntary tips would be excluded from taxable income.

analysis.who_pays: Recipients of the programs left unprotected — Medicaid, food assistance, housing, education, and transportation — would bear spending cuts of up to 15%, since only Social Security, Medicare, and veterans' programs were carved out. Workers and consumers would also absorb the 15% business levy, which functions like a consumption tax passed into prices, and would lose deductions and credits like the child credit and charitable deduction.

drawbacks.text: Direct-spending cuts of up to 15% would fall on everything not exempted — Medicaid, food assistance, and other programs lower-income households depend on — because only Social Security, Medicare, and veterans' programs were protected.
The 15% tax on business income is designed like a consumption tax: businesses would pass it into prices, and price increases take the largest share out of lower-income budgets.

Working households would lose common deductions and credits — charitable giving, state and local taxes, child credits — and new homebuyers would get no mortgage interest deduction at all; only pre-existing mortgages were grandfathered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Even a friendly reading shows the trade running one way: the biggest tax cuts went to capital income and inheritances, while the bill paid for them by cutting non-exempt spending and by taxing consumption, which weighs heaviest on the poor. A middle-class worker would likely see a modest tax cut; a retiree on Medicaid, a family relying on food assistance, or anyone using domestic discretionary programs would bear the offset. The exemption floor and tax-free tips were real benefits for low-wage workers, but they are small next to the estate-tax repeal and the untaxed investment income at the top.

outcome.mechanism: Helms introduced it alone with no cosponsors; the Senate Finance Committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, and it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jesse Helms introduced the Flat Tax Act of 1995 on July 14, 1995 and gave introductory remarks on the floor.
Not a single senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
It expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing progressive tax code and 1995 spending levels carried on: Medicaid, food assistance, domestic programs, and the estate tax all survived untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicaid, food aid, and the estate tax survived

for.name: Jesse Helms
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it had no other sponsor or cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on its introduction day and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Helms, a Republican, was the bill's only backer — zero senators of either party cosponsored and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have erased taxes on capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritances while cutting the top wage rate to 15%. The offset was 15% cuts to domestic spending and a consumption-style business levy, shifting the burden toward work and lower-income households.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software firms
industries.note: A 15% flat rate with almost no deductions, plus abolishing the IRS, would shrink the market for paid filing help. The public-side counterpart is a far simpler, cheaper tax filing process.
Repealing all deductions would eliminate the charitable deduction, likely reducing giving and forcing nonprofits to cut services the public relies on.
Mortgage interest would no longer be deductible for new home purchases; only pre-existing mortgages were grandfathered, removing a subsidy that had supported home demand.
